svg.text: Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207) for a digital power substation, from the field devices to the control centre. Being on the network grants nothing: every request carries a verifiable identity, is judged by policy and a live trust score, and is enforced before it
reaches anything that matters. Follow the numbered steps 1 to 6 for one full cycle.

Every device is simulated by ztc-edge and has its own identity, for example spiffe://grid.example/edge/pmu/pmu-b1-1.
One full cycle, in six steps
A device proves that it may join with a one-time join token, and gets a short-lived certificate with its own identity from the identity provider. Like everything that leaves the
substation, the request passes the firewall.
Every request the device sends carries that certificate. It goes over the field network to the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), which checks it with mutual TLS.
The PEP first looks for a recent answer in its decision cache. If there is none, it asks the Policy Engine in the control centre through the firewall. The answer combines the
policy with the device's current trust score, and the audit log records it.
Only allowed requests are passed on to the fog node. A denied request stops at the PEP.
The intrusion detection system gets a copy of the field traffic from the fog node. When a device behaves suspiciously, it sends a trust signal through the broker, and the
The Policy Administrator announces a new revocation epoch through the firewall. Every PEP clears its cached answers, so the device's next request is decided again with the

An arrow that ends at the firewall or the broker carries on out of the other side, with the same number and style. Nothing
crosses the DMZ any other way.

If no decision can be made, the answer is no. An
attacker who cuts the WAN must not be able to switch
access control off. Availability comes from where
decisions are made, not from weaker failure modes.
One zone model, enforced four times
IEC 62443 zones and conduits are defined once and
exported to Kubernetes network policies, Docker
networks, Cisco ACLs and OpenStack security groups.

govulncheck, gosec, gitleaks and Trivy, and ships as a
small non-root image with an SBOM.
